content: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is an autosomal recessive disorder that results in a deficiency of glucocorticoids and is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in pediatric populations. In over 90% of cases, the condition is caused by a deficiency in the 21-hydroxylase enzyme, which is due to mutations in the 21-hydroxylase gene. Management of CAH caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency involves oral glucocorticoid replacement therapy, such as hydrocortisone or prednisolone, to suppress adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels. Additionally, mineralocorticoid replacement is required to prevent salt-wasting complications. In children, the primary goals of treatment are to prevent adrenal crises, achieve normal growth and development, optimize adult height, and ensure normal pubertal progression. In adults, the focus shifts to preventing adrenal crises, maintaining normal fertility, and avoiding long-term complications associated with glucocorticoid therapy. However, current glucocorticoid regimens are unable to fully replicate the physiological cortisol rhythm, leading to frequent reports of over-treatment or under-treatment. The objective of this study was to compare the efficacy and safety of various glucocorticoid replacement regimens in children and adults with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. A systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register, supplemented by searches of trial registries, reference lists, and conference abstracts. The last search was performed on June 24, 2019. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared different glucocorticoid replacement regimens in children and adults with CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by the authors, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The search identified 1,729 records, of which 43 were further examined. Ultimately, five RCTs (six references) involving 101 participants were included, with an additional six ongoing RCTs identified. The trials included participants aged 3.6 months to 21 years, with sample sizes ranging from six to 44 participants. Four trials used a cross-over design, while one employed a parallel design. Treatment durations ranged from two weeks to six months per treatment arm, with overall follow-up periods of six to 12 months. The trials were judged to have a moderate to high risk of bias due to insufficient methodological details. All trials utilized oral glucocorticoid replacement therapy but varied in dosing schedules and levels. Three trials compared different hydrocortisone (HC) dosing schedules, one trial compared HC, prednisolone (PD), and dexamethasone (DXA) in a three-arm design, and one trial compared HC with fludrocortisone to PD with fludrocortisone. Due to the heterogeneity of the trials and limited evidence, meta-analyses could not be performed. None of the trials reported on quality of life, prevention of adrenal crises, presence of osteopenia, testicular or ovarian adrenal rest tumors, subfertility, or final adult height. Five trials reported on androgen normalization using various measurements, but the evidence quality was very low. Five trials measured 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) levels, four measured androstenedione, three measured testosterone, and one measured dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS). One trial with 15 participants found that high morning or evening doses of HC made little to no difference in 17-OHP, testosterone, androstenedione, or DHEAS levels after four weeks. Another trial with 27 participants found that HC and DXA suppressed 17-OHP and androstenedione more effectively than PD after six weeks. A third trial with eight participants reported no differences in 17-OHP levels across five HC dosing schedules over four to six weeks. A trial with 44 participants comparing HC and PD found no differences in 17-OHP, androstenedione, or testosterone levels after one year. Another trial with 26 participants comparing HC alone to HC plus fludrocortisone found that HC alone suppressed 17-OHP and androstenedione more effectively at six months, but no differences were observed in testosterone levels. While no trials reported final adult height, surrogate markers were assessed. Three trials reported on growth and bone maturation, and two trials reported on height velocity. One trial found that height velocity was reduced at six months in participants receiving HC 25 mg/m²/day compared to HC 15 mg/m²/day, both with fludrocortisone, but the evidence quality was very low, making it unclear if the HC dose caused the difference. No differences were observed in growth hormone or IGF-1 levels. Another trial with 44 participants found no differences in growth velocity between HC and PD after one year, but suggested that PD may provide better control of bone maturation in prepubertal children. The HC group showed a higher absolute change in the bone age-to-chronological age ratio compared to the PD group. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence comparing the efficacy and safety of different glucocorticoid regimens for treating CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency in children and adults. No trials examined long-term outcomes such as quality of life, prevention of adrenal crises, osteopenia, testicular or ovarian adrenal rest tumors, subfertility, or final adult height. Additionally, no studies evaluated modified-release hydrocortisone formulations or 24-hour circadian continuous subcutaneous hydrocortisone infusion. As a result, uncertainty remains regarding the optimal glucocorticoid replacement therapy for CAH. Future trials should include both pediatric and adult populations and incorporate longer follow-up periods to assess biochemical and clinical outcomes comprehensively.
